reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: A varicocele is an abnormal dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus, classically described as feeling like a bag of worms on scrotal palpation
The great majority occur on the left side, attributed to the left testicular vein draining at a right angle into the left renal vein and having a longer course
It is more prominent on standing and with Valsalva and typically decompresses on lying down; a varicocele that does not empty when supine should raise concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass
A sudden new right-sided or non-reducing varicocele in an older patient warrants imaging to exclude a renal tumour obstructing venous drainage
Clinical grading ranges from subclinical (detectable only on imaging) to visible through the scrotal skin, with intermediate grades palpable with or without Valsalva

Varicoceles are a common and potentially reversible factor in male subfertility, associated with impaired sperm count, motility, and morphology, and sometimes with testicular growth arrest in adolescents

Most are asymptomatic or cause a dull dragging ache; treatment (surgical varicocelectomy or radiological embolisation) is considered for pain, infertility with abnormal semen analysis, or testicular growth failure in adolescents
Semen analysis and assessment of testicular volume guide management decisions in the fertility and adolescent contexts
reference.pathophysiology: A varicocele results from incompetent or absent valves in the internal spermatic (testicular) veins, leading to retrograde flow and dilatation of the pampiniform plexus. The predominance on the left relates to the anatomy of left testicular venous drainage into the left renal vein at a right angle with a longer, higher-pressure course. The resulting venous stasis is thought to impair testicular function through elevated scrotal temperature, venous hypertension, hypoxia, and reflux of adrenal or renal metabolites, contributing to defective spermatogenesis and, in some cases, testicular atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Retroperitoneal or renal mass obstructing venous drainage (secondary varicocele)
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal examination in both standing and supine positions with Valsalva
Scrotal colour Doppler ultrasound to confirm venous reflux and grade the varicocele
Measurement of testicular volume to detect growth arrest, especially in adolescents
Semen analysis in men presenting with subfertility
Abdominal/renal imaging when a right-sided, isolated, or non-reducing varicocele suggests a retroperitoneal cause
redFlags: New-onset right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele suggesting a renal or retroperitoneal tumour
Progressive ipsilateral testicular atrophy or growth arrest in an adolescent
Acute painful scrotal swelling raising alternative diagnoses that require exclusion
Significant deterioration in semen parameters in a man seeking fertility
reference.prognosis: Many varicoceles are asymptomatic and require no intervention; when treated for pain, subfertility, or adolescent growth arrest, repair often improves semen parameters and testicular growth, though not all men achieve improved fertility.
pitfalls: Failing to examine the patient standing and with Valsalva, missing a lower-grade varicocele
Overlooking a secondary varicocele from a renal tumour in an isolated right-sided or non-reducible case
Recommending repair for asymptomatic subclinical varicoceles without a clear indication
Neglecting testicular volume assessment in adolescents
Attributing subfertility solely to the varicocele without full evaluation of both partners
management: Reassure and observe asymptomatic subclinical or low-grade varicoceles that are not affecting fertility or testicular growth, without intervention

Offer varicocele repair by microsurgical subinguinal ligation or radiological percutaneous venous embolisation for chronic scrotal pain, subfertility with abnormal semen parameters, or adolescent testicular growth arrest
Provide symptomatic relief with scrotal support and simple analgesia for aching discomfort
Monitor with serial semen analysis in subfertile men and serial testicular volume or ultrasound in adolescents to detect catch-up growth or ongoing arrest
Image the retroperitoneum and kidneys for an isolated right-sided or non-reducing varicocele to exclude an obstructing renal or retroperitoneal tumour
Refer to urology and, where subfertility persists, to reproductive medicine for assisted conception
Review after repair for recurrence and for postoperative hydrocele
